questions.title: Why does GRPO’s token‑level importance weight violate the principle of importance sampling?
questions.question_body: In the GRPO objective (Eq. 2) the importance ratio is defined as \(w_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid x, y_{i,<t})}\). The paper claims this is a mis‑application of importance sampling because it is computed on a single token sample rather than an average over many samples. Could someone explain in detail how the standard importance sampling identity works for sequence‑level distributions and why applying it token‑wise leads to a biased or high‑variance estimator? A concrete example with a short sequence would be helpful.

questions.title: How is the sequence‑level importance ratio \(s_i(\theta)\) derived and why is length normalization used?
questions.question_body:
GSPO defines \(s_i(\theta)=\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_i|x)}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(y_i|x)}\right)^{1/|y_i|}=\exp\left(\frac{1}{|y_i|}\sum_{t}\log \frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{old}}(y_{i,t}|x,y_{i,<t})}\right)\).
Why do the authors raise the likelihood ratio to the power \(1/|y_i|\)? How does this length normalization affect the scale of the ratio and the clipping range? Would it be possible to omit this step, and if so, what practical issues would arise?

questions.title: What exactly is the “group‑based advantage” \(\widehat{A}_i\) and how is it computed in practice?
questions.question_body:
Both GRPO and GSPO use \(\widehat{A}_i = \frac{r(x,y_i)-\mathrm{mean}(\{r(x,y_j)\}_{j=1}^G)}{\mathrm{std}(\{r(x,y_j)\}_{j=1}^G)}\).
I am confused about a few details: (1) Is the standard deviation computed across the whole group for each query separately? (2) What happens if all rewards in a group are identical (zero std)? (3) Are rewards ever normalized further (e.g., to keep them within [‑1, 1]) before being used as advantages?

questions.title: Why does clipping a larger fraction of tokens in GSPO still lead to higher training efficiency than GRPO?
questions.question_body: Figure 3 in the paper shows that GSPO clips two orders of magnitude more tokens than GRPO, yet its sample efficiency is better. Intuitively, discarding more data should hurt learning. Can someone clarify why sequence‑level clipping provides a cleaner learning signal despite using fewer token‑level gradients? Is this related to variance reduction of the importance weights or to alignment between reward granularity and optimization unit?

questions.title: How does expert‑activation volatility in MoE models break GRPO’s token‑level importance ratios?
questions.question_body: The authors report that after a gradient update, about 10 % of the experts activated for a given token change, causing large fluctuations in \(w_{i,t}(\theta)\. Why does a change in expert routing affect the token probability ratio so dramatically? Is this because different experts have vastly different output distributions, or because routing decisions are not differentiable? How does GSPO avoid this problem by using only sequence likelihoods?

questions.title: What is the ‘Routing Replay’ strategy and why does it add memory/communication overhead?
questions.question_body: In Section 5.4 the paper mentions caching the routing decisions of \(\pi_{\theta_{old}}\) and replaying them when computing \(w_{i,t}(\theta)\. I would like to understand exactly how this works: (a) what information needs to be stored per token (expert IDs, gating scores?), (b) how is it re‑used during the forward pass of \(\pi_θ\), and (c) why does this increase memory usage compared to standard forward passes? Also, does Routing Replay interfere with learning new routing patterns?

questions.title: Can GSPO be applied to multi‑turn RL without modification?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces GSPO‑token as a token‑level variant for multi‑turn settings where per‑token advantages may be needed. If I have a dialogue where each turn receives its own reward, should I use GSPO‑token with separate \(\widehat{A}_{i,t}\) for each turn, or can I still apply plain GSPO by aggregating turn rewards into a single sequence reward? What are the trade‑offs in terms of stability and credit assignment?

questions.title: Why does GSPO allow direct use of inference‑engine likelihoods despite precision mismatches?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that because GSPO uses only sequence‑level likelihoods, it tolerates precision differences between training (e.g., fp16 on Megatron) and inference engines (e.g., fp32 on vLLM). How significant are these precision discrepancies for token‑wise versus sequence‑wise likelihoods? Is there any empirical evidence that using inference probabilities directly does not degrade performance, or is this just an intuition?

questions.title: How does the gradient expression in Eq. (9) differ qualitatively from that of GRPO?
questions.question_body: In Eq. (9) the gradient contains a factor \(s_i(θ) = (π_θ(y_i|x)/π_{θ_{old}}(y_i|x))^{1/|y_i|}\) multiplied by an average over token log‑gradients. In contrast, GRPO’s gradient weights each token by its own importance ratio \(w_{i,t}(θ)\. Could someone walk through a simple numerical example (e.g., two tokens, two responses) showing how these two gradients behave differently when one token’s probability changes drastically while the other stays stable?

questions..title: "What hyperparameters control the clipping range in GSPO versus GRPO and how should they be tuned?"
questions..question_body: "The paper uses clipping ranges of [3e-4, 4e-4] for GSPO and [0.2, 0.27] for GRPO. Since these numbers differ by orders of magnitude, how do I choose appropriate values for a new dataset? Should I first look at typical values of \(s_i(θ)\. Are there any recommended heuristics or validation procedures to set ε for sequence‑level clipping?"
